You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

=== TEXT A ===
# Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

Every product organization has a roadmap, and most of them are fiction. Not malicious fiction—aspirational fiction. They promise features on dates nobody can honestly guarantee, and within a quarter or two, reality has usually made other plans. The failure isn't in execution; it's baked into how roadmaps are conceived.

The deepest flaw is that roadmaps confuse outputs with outcomes. A typical roadmap is a list of features: a dashboard in Q2, an integration in Q3. But features are solutions to problems we haven't necessarily validated. Committing to a solution months in advance assumes we already know what will work—an assumption that survives contact with actual customers maybe half the time. Teams then ship to satisfy the document rather than solve the problem, becoming what product thinker John Cutler calls a "feature factory": busy, productive, and strategically irrelevant.

Worse, roadmaps are rarely products of evidence; they're products of negotiation. Sales needs a commitment to close a deal. An executive has a pet idea. A competitor launched something, so it goes on the list. The resulting artifact reflects internal power dynamics more than customer insight—which is why so many roadmap items die quietly after launch. They were never wanted by anyone outside the building.

Then there's the problem of time. Roadmaps imply a certainty about the future that doesn't exist. Software estimation is notoriously unreliable, and the further out a plan extends, the more it resembles astrology. Markets shift, assumptions break, learning accumulates—yet the roadmap, refreshed quarterly at best, sits frozen like a photograph of a moving scene. Teams keep marching toward stale priorities because updating the plan feels like admitting failure.

Underneath all of this usually lies a missing strategy. A roadmap without strategy is just a compromise document: something for every stakeholder, excellence for no one. Real strategy means choosing what *not* to do, and most roadmaps conspicuously avoid that choice.

The fix isn't to abandon roadmaps but to change what they are. Effective teams organize roadmaps around problems and outcomes rather than features and dates. They use horizons like *now / next / later* instead of false-precision timelines. They treat each item as a hypothesis to be tested, not a promise to be kept, and they revise continuously as they learn. In short, they treat the roadmap as a living statement of bets—humble about the future, ruthless about priorities, and accountable to results rather than to the plan itself.

A roadmap should be a compass, not a contract. Most fail because organizations insist on the opposite.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
**Most product roadmaps fail because they confuse planning with prediction, outputs with outcomes, and internal politics with customer value.**

A product roadmap is meant to communicate direction: what problems the team will solve, roughly when, and why it matters. In practice, many become Gantt charts of features with dates, treated as contracts. Stakeholders treat dates as promises; teams treat them as commitments. Reality—new customer evidence, competitive moves, technical surprises, or capacity limits—then turns the document into a source of missed expectations and eroded trust. The failure is not that plans change; it is that the organization never treated the roadmap as a hypothesis that would be revised.

A second common failure is output-obsession. Roadmaps list features (“redesign checkout,” “add AI search”) rather than outcomes (“reduce cart abandonment by X,” “increase successful searches among new users”). Without a clear problem and success metric, teams ship work that looks busy but does not move the business. Discovery is often thin or after-the-fact: personas, interviews, and experiments happen too late or not at all, so the roadmap encodes assumptions instead of evidence. Prioritization then defaults to the loudest voice, the biggest customer, or the next quarter’s demo rather than impact versus effort.

Alignment is equally fragile. Engineering, design, sales, support, and leadership often do not share the same understanding of strategy or constraints. A roadmap that is not co-created or regularly socialized becomes a private artifact of the product team. Dependencies, technical debt, and capacity are ignored or underestimated, producing an overcommitted plan. When the plan inevitably slips, blame replaces learning.

Finally, many roadmaps are static. Markets, users, and technology do not wait for the next annual planning cycle. Teams that cannot re-prioritize without drama, or that lack a lightweight “now / next / later” structure, either freeze in place or thrash. The document stops being a decision tool and becomes theater.

Roadmaps that work are shorter on dates and longer on problems, evidence, and intended outcomes. They are living, visible, and revised as learning arrives. They connect strategy to sequenced bets rather than to a feature factory. Most fail not because planning is useless, but because organizations use the artifact to avoid the harder work of discovery, trade-offs, and honest communication.
=== END OF TEXT B ===
